utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Registrar. Could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, madam. I just want to make sure that all the accused are receiving interpretation. I see Mr. Sarapa is not here. More or less the rest of the teams are okay, except Mr. Ostojic is also not here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. May it please the Trial Chamber. Mr. Ostojic is on business in Belgrade and should be back Wednesday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. And from the Prosecution there's Mr. McCloskey, okay. So Mr. Thayer, will you be leading the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes I will, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Are there any preliminaries you would like to raise? I thank you. I hear none. As we intimated to you earlier on two weeks ago before -- when we had the last sitting, the very first thing we will proceed with today is a short proces verbal dealing or illustrating the site visit that the Trial Chamber conducted between the 2nd and the 7th of October. The decision to hold a site visit was originated from the Trial Chamber and was supported by both parties. Preparations were undertaken months ago in order to make it possible, and during the various 65 ter meetings that took place a list of rules of conduct to be observed during the site visit was agreed to by the parties. Basically, the rules of conduct which were agreed to by the parties and which were observed in the course of the entire site visit were the following: First, the parties, particularly since the accused were not going to be present for the site visit, the parties would not seek the admission of evidence through the entire duration of the site visit. I can confirm that none of the parties sought the admission of evidence. It was also agreed that the guide, who was Mr. Philip Berikoff, would only indicate to the Judges and the parties geographic locations without giving any running commentary regarding events which are alleged to have occurred there. However, it was also agreed that this would not exclude specific references to paragraphs of the indictment which refer to these locations. Again, I'd like to thank Mr. Berikoff for having observed this rule of conduct throughout the entire site visit. And as far as the parties themselves were concerned, the terms of reference or the rules of conduct agreed upon were the following: During the site visit, the parties would not give any views or offer advice or express an opinion or make any other comment in relation to the locations visited unless requested to do so by the Judges. The parties could, however, agree amongst themselves to address observations to the Judges when they were relevant to a better understanding of the locations visit. Also, more or less this rule of conduct was observed by all parties. Now, the -- all the Judges of this Trial Chamber, the four of us, took part in this site visit and at all times we were accompanied by two members of the Chamber legal staff, one representative of the Registry. On the Prosecution's side, there was Mr. Peter McCloskey, who was the chief trial attorney in this case, and he was assisted by Kweku Vanderpuye and investigator Tomasz Blasczyk. And the various Defence teams were each represented by one counsel; namely, Mr. Zivanovic for Popovic, Christopher Meek for Beara, Jelena Nikolic for Mr. Nikolic, Miodrag Stojanovic for Borovcanin, Natacha Faveau Ivanovic for Militic, Dragan Krgovic for Mr. Gvero and Georgia Sarapa for accused Pandurevic. As I intimated earlier on, the guide who was agreed upon by both parties was Mr. Phil Berikoff. The purpose of the site visit was of course to view some of the sites which are relevant to the case before us. Some of the sites were selected by the Trial Chamber, others were indicated by the parties. Unfortunately because of time constraints and also weather conditions and terrain conditions there were some proposed sites that we could not visit. These were mainly or almost exclusively exhumation -- exhumation sites, but this -- these sites were not visited upon agreement by all parties. The -- we started the -- visiting places on the 2nd of October. On the 3rd of October, driving from Sarajevo to Gorazde, passing through Trnovo, Foca and Ustikolina and Gorazde, we saw the UNPROFOR -- previous UNPROFOR check-point. And then we passed through Borik, seeing the Borik school and the forward command post of the VRS Rogatica brigade, moved on to Zepa, where we saw the site of the former location of the Ukrainian contingent of UNPROFOR. Crna Rijeka where we saw the former installation of the Crna Rijeka military installation of Crna Rijeka. And that first day ended with a visit to the Han Pijesak where we saw both the Drina Corps Main Staff headquarters, in other words, where they were, and the restaurant where allegedly party to General Zivanovic was held. On the second day, that's on the 4th of October, we went to Milici where we saw the medical centre, to Zeleni Jadar and to secondary burial sites, moved on to Javor where we saw where the 1st Tactical Group 1 position allegedly was. Then to Pribicevac, where we saw the observation post of the Drina Corps or of the former Drina Corps forward command post. And we moved to Srebrenica where we walked through the town itself. Saw the location of the municipal courthouse, the PTT building, the Bravo compound location, the gas station which we have seen in one of the videos, and former location of the destroyed mosque, amongst other things. Moved on to Potocari where we saw the location the Zinc Factory Energo building and the "White House," the UN Canadian DutchBat Compound, and observation post Papa, and also the Yellow Bridge at Zuti Most together with a view of Kokarda hill. We moved on to Bratunac where we saw the locations of the brick factory, the hotel Fontana which we saw from the inside, the SDS building, the police station, the old Vuk Karadzic school, the old school also known as the technical school, the soccer field, and the Bratunac Brigade headquarters, military police building locations. We drove on to the Glogova sites where we saw the Glogova primary grave sites that are referred to by the Prosecution. In Kravica, we saw the market, the site of the market, the school. We didn't stop there. And also Kravica warehouse where we stopped and also went in. We stopped at Sandici meadow and saw the school and the gas station at Konjevic Polje and the soccer field and the school in Nova -- Nova Kasaba. On the 5th of October, we went to Pilica where we saw the cultural centre and the Kula school, together with the restaurant that is in front of the cultural centre. Branjevo where we saw the site where the Branjevo Military Farm was situated. Rocevic is alleged to have been situated, Rocevic where we saw the school, Kozluk. We were shown by the Prosecution a site where an alleged execution is -- is -- was mentioned. This alleged execution site is by the Drina River. We saw the site of the Vitinka bottling company factory and the -- also the Drina Corps headquarters. In Petkovic -- Petkovci we saw the school and also the old school said to be the former Zvornik brigade 6th Battalion headquarters. We also went to the Petkovci dam. We moved on to Zvornik where we saw the Zvornik Brigade headquarters, to Orahovac where we saw the Grbavci, Orahovac school and also the alleged Orahovac Rensen execution sites. We moved on to did Delici and to Baljkovica. In Delici we saw the command post of the 4th Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade and the forward command post of the Zvornik Brigade. And in Baljkovica we visited an area which was indicated to us by the Defence for Pandurevic. On the 6th of October, which was the last day of the site visit, we went to the Jadar River where we saw a site indicated to us by the Prosecution. Cerska village, we saw an alleged execution and grave site. Nova Kasaba we went there again to see a primary mass grave site indicated to us by the Prosecution. And the last place visited by the Trial Chamber and the rest of the party was at Tiska where we saw the location of the Luka school. Site visit concluded on Friday, 6th December [sic], and the Trial Chamber returned to The Hague on Sunday. Before closing, I -- Trial Chamber, and I'm speaking for the entire Trial Chamber, would like to thank the President of this Tribunal for having authorised this site visit, the Registrar for having made it possible, Mr. Phil Berikoff, acting chief of security, for having organised the entire site visit and for having accepted to serve as guide, the precious ICTY security services members that accompanied the entire delegation. They were -- they did an excellent job. The civilian authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and especially the security services operating in the areas visited both in Republika Srpska and in the federation -- federation. We will -- the Trial Chamber will be forwarding -- will be sending formal letters of thanks to all the authorities on land there as well as to the representatives of this Tribunal in Sarajevo on in Banja Luka who assisted Mr. Berikoff in preparing the site visit. I have got nothing else to say, just instruct that what I have stated on behalf of the Trial Chamber is entered into the records as a proces verbal. However, before we start with the rest of our business today, I'd like to know if any of the parties, Prosecution and any of the Defence teams, would like to make any comments on the site visit. Same applies to the accused in case you would like any information or you'd like to put any questions. I'll start with you, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Mr. President and Your Honours. Just two very brief slight corrections to your list. In Han Pijesak is the headquarters of the Main Staff, not the -- not the Drina Corps headquarters. I think that was just a typo in Mr. Berikoff's material. The headquarters of the Drina Corps is actually in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the -- also the headquarters building next to the Vitinka factory in Kozluk is the headquarters of the Drina Wolves, and otherwise that was just right, and that's all I would have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you so much for those corrections, which I'm sure everyone will agree with. Any remarks, comments from the Defence teams? I see none. Would any of the accused like to put any questions or seek any information? I see none. So I think we can pass on to the rest of our agenda. We know that there are various motions that have been filed. We will be dealing with them one by one, not necessarily in the way they have been filed because some are more urgent than others, and we will let you know exactly what our projected time schedule is later on today or tomorrow. Can we bring the witness in, Mr. Colonel Franken. Is he still in the Dutch army or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. He is retired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, to you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal once more. You know what the procedure is, so I will not be explaining to you. Madam Usher, who is standing to your left, will be handing to you the text of a solemn declaration that our rules require you to make before you start giving evidence. It's legally and morally binding, the same way as an oath is. Please proceed with making the declaration, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us that you will be testifying the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Make yourself comfortable, please. Colonel, I know that you have retired from the Dutch -- Royal Dutch Army. How would you like me to address you here, like us to address you, as Colonel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir, I am a civilian now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are a civilian now. All right. So, Mr. Franken, Mr. Thayer will be examining you in chief, at least today and possibly -- Do you think you will finish today? You'll try.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will do my best. I honestly believe we'll go just a little bit into the first session tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. And in the meantime during either the first or the second break, whoever is coordinating will give us an updated idea on how much time you think the Defence teams will require for cross-examination. All right? Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We will be speaking the same language. However, what we say is going to be translated into a couple of languages, so I would just ask that you speak a little bit more slowly than normal, as I will try as well, and I would also ask you to just pause slightly before your answer whether it's me asking the question or my learned colleagues or Their Honours. All right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you please state and spell your name.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: My name is Robert Franken, and that is Foxtrot-Romeo-Alpha-November-Kilo-Echo-November. Franken.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how old you, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: I am 56 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if I may, I would just like to review briefly your military service history with you. You are a former infantry officer of the Royal Netherlands Army, retiring after 33 years of service with the rank of colonel; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And among your positions during that time you commanded a combat support company, commanded a mechanised infantry company?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Served as an operations officer in an armoured brigade with responsibility for planning and executing air support?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You served as a tactics instructor at the infantry school --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, Mr. Franken, it's both of you, actually, if you could kindly slow down a little bit. Just allow a short pause between question and answer. That's all you need to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Will do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You served as a logistics and intelligence officer at battalion and brigade level?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you served as Chief of Staff of northern command in Holland as well?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct as well, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Have I left anything out, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Not of any importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, when you entered on duty in Bosnia, what was your rank and what was your position at that time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: I was a major. My -- my position was DCO and S4; that is, the officer responsible for logistics of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I'll ask you some questions about that in a moment. When did you actually arrive in Bosnia, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: As far as I recollect, it was the 15th of January in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And where were you physically based?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: At Potocari, headquarters of DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just briefly, sir. What did you understand the mission of DutchBat III to be?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Our mission was to deter any hostile action by being present, showing our presence, showing the flag, as we will called it. We had to facilitate and to assist in -- in humanitarian aid. The mission was as well to demilitarise the -- the enclave, so that's about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you referred to your position as being the DCO of DutchBat. What does DCO stand for, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Sorry. It's deputy commanding officer. So popularly said, the second in command.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And who was your immediate commander?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You mentioned a moment ago that you were the S4 in charge of logistics. Could you just briefly describe what that entailed?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That means you're responsible for all the supplies and spare parts a battalion needs for -- for being operational in an area like that. So it includes food, fuel, MO, spare parts, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in your position as DCO, would you actually stand in for the commander if he were absent for some reason?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: In general, sir, would -- would you describe the division of responsibilities between yourself and Colonel Karremans.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah, in fact, the colonel was doing all the external contacts, so contacts with higher echelons, and I was doing, yeah, more or less the daily commanding of the battalion, so the normal routine things. I was coordinating the staff and giving the company commanders orders within the guidelines, of course, of Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And was there some central entity which assisted you in terms of keeping informed about what was going on throughout the battalion, given your many duties during the day?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: There was an operations room. You could call that the nerve centre of the battalion where all the information came in and the crew of that operations room had all the, what you say, disciplines in it, in the crew. So they analysed the information and gave me their results or their conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And generally would there be a particular officer in the operations room who would be transmitting you the information?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. Was the chief operations room duty officer was always a captain, and he is the one that contacted me, and if there was anything of -- of interest that I should know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, were there particular VRS and army of Bosnia and Herzegovina officers with whom you had contact in connection with your duties?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. There was the formal liaison of the Bosnian Serb army was a Colonel Vukovic. I saw him very little. But in fact there was a Major Nikolic of the Bratunac Brigade who actually was our liaison to the Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in terms of the army of the Bosnia-Herzegovina, were there any particular officers with whom you had more frequent contact?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah, well, the contacts to the Bosnian army was through the Chief of Staff of the 28th Division, Ramiz, the man I know as Ramiz. And eventually in the beginning we contact of course with Oric, the local commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you know what this commander Oric's first name was, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: I was, but I can't recollect it right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, was there within DutchBat a -- an S5 or liaison officer who served as the primary liaison with these individuals?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: There was a team of liaison officers. In fact, there were three in the beginning at least, and they did the contact as well to the Serbs as to the Bosnian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Given that you had those officers available, sir, under what circumstances, generally speaking, would you become involved with these officers of the VRS or army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, when the S5 couldn't cope with the problem or didn't come any further in the results then I would come in and do the talking and the negotiations with them. And when I did fail, the last trick we had was that the colonel himself came in.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, during your service with DutchBat III, did you have an opportunity to observe soldiers of both of the opposing armies in terms of uniforms, equipment, and so forth?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And would you start with the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, please, and just describe in general terms how they were equipped.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, they -- they didn't wear their weapons because that was forbidden, but we -- from intelligence and information from our predecessors we knew that they had about 4, 4.500 small arms and some mortars, and what you could see of it that they were mostly -- most of the time walking around in, yeah, parts of uniforms, never dressed up completely. That changed somewhere in May. Then we saw suddenly that there were new combat suits worn by the BiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you have an opportunity to observe how that army operated in terms of cohesion and discipline and centralised command?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, there was a divisional structure. There was a division command with brigades who had all their own area within the enclave. So it looked like an army, but it proved pretty soon that -- that there was no discipline. The brigade commanders had their own policies. They -- they did not obey to what the division commander said or wanted. An example is the brigade commander in the Bandera Triangle who had his own army. And, well, especially in the end phase we had to cope with local commanders with their own policies who did not follow the orders of the Bosnian divisional command. So to say it was more or less a bunch of armed militia partly doing and functioning as a whole but mostly on their own there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'd like to turn your attention to the VRS. Could you describe your experiences and observations in terms of that army in the same manner you just described the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, please.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: We had to deal with a couple of brigades. With the Skelani brigade and Bratunac Brigade, we had contact in the Milici area never. That looked like an army. Orders were given. It was clearly that officers gave orders and they were done as you usually see in an army. The troops around the enclave were more or less, with exception of the Milici Brigade, militia-like, combinations of uniforms, et cetera, but they had heavy weapons. In the end phase, we were confronted twice with military units looking and acting like absolute military units as we knew them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, although you were the DCO and responsible for logistics for DutchBat, would you also participate yourself in patrols?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. I did about 23 or -- patrols myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And were patrols around the enclave part of DutchBat's regular activities?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And were you able to observe positions of both Serb and Muslim forces personally during the course --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- of your patrols?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did your observations include trenches?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. On the Bosnian -- yeah, on both sides there were trenches. On the Serb side there were bunker-like buildings. Trenches on Bosnian side were -- were pretty shallow, not deep, and the positions on the Serb side were, as far as we could see, pretty well dug out and firm.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: How about fixed artillery positions, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, we had identified about - in the beginning, at least - 16 artillery and mortar positions, especially in the area of the Milici Brigade that is on the west side of the enclave. There were a couple of positions of self-propelled mechanised guns, artillery that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And to which army did those positions belong, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to turn your attention to another topic for a few moments, sir. In the months prior to the VRS attack on the enclave in July of 1995, was there shelling and shooting into the enclave?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Was there also firing at DutchBat patrols or positions?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. There was an increasing amount of what we call close firing on patrols and on our operation -- sorry, observation points.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we'll get to that in a moment, sir. But while we're on the topic, do you recall approximately when that increase in firing incidents began to happen?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That was as of April. April, May it started to increase. Well, it increased until the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what was the source of those firing incidents, in terms of which army?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Reported was mostly it was done by the Serb -- out of the Serb positions. There are a couple of reports where the source of the firing was not destined, was not known, but it was majorly from the Bosnian Serb positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you personally come under fire during any of your patrols by fire from the Serb positions?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, a couple of times.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: How else would you learn about shelling and shooting incidents?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Reports by patrols or by the observation posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you ever observe or receive reports about the results of the shelling or shooting incidents on -- on the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, several times they were wounded, the civil population. We used our means, our armoured ambulances, so to say, to bring the people to the hospital in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, did you have freedom of movement in the Serb territory?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Within the Serb territory, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how about free movement by the Muslim forces within the enclave?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah, with exception of what we call the Bandera Triangle, an area in the west side of the enclave, we were supposed to have freedom of movement. I say supposed to, because in the end we had lots of trouble moving our APCs to better positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And so you have some personal experience in terms of restriction on freedom of movement in the Bandera Triangle; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Would you just briefly share with the Court that experience?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. There was already non-freedom of movement when we arrived, when we took over from DutchBat II, and we got in January, yes, orders to restore that freedom of movement in that area. And I let the first patrol into the Bandera Triangle, and that -- well, we got some skirmishing and -- and problems with the BiH. I was stopped by about 45 armed men to enter the area. Other patrols were stopped as well, and it ended in a blockade, more or less, during a couple of days where we had to stay in the area. We couldn't return to camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I want to turn your attention now to another area, sir, involving your role as the chief logistics officer for the battalion. You've testified that part of your responsibilities was to be aware of the battalion's resupply needs. What were the most important items requiring resupply for DutchBat?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: In fact, ammo and fuel, because we had to raise our energy, any energy, all by ourselves, and the only way to do that was with generators and they ran on diesel.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I take it, sir, that the battalion's logistical needs were passed up the UNPROFOR chain of command?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how was that done?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: By fax. We made lists and requested supplies, of course food, et cetera, as well, but requested the -- the supplies and it was sent to -- to Sarajevo and then over to Zagreb where there was a major log base, and they were preparing that. There was a log base at Busovaca, there was a Dutch unit as well, and they loaded this stuff we wanted on trucks, at least that was the general idea, and then bring it to us by road.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: When you say "log base," are you referring to a logistics base?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Sorry. A logistics base, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, did the VRS become involved in this process of resupply requests?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. For every convoy, there had to be admission by the VRS. They had to consent that. Not only the fact that vehicles were driving down to us, but they wanted to know exactly what was in the vehicles and did approve or not approve the contents of the trucks and the amount of trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And to your knowledge did the VRS become involved in the actual approval of the lists that were sent over?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- from the UNPROFOR logistics personnel?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. They had to approve every little item on the list, whether that it was allowed to bring it in or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Were there items which the VRS categorically denied?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. Ammunition anyway. Anything that had to do with weapons systems, spare parts or testing devices. Spare parts for vehicles, et cetera, were denied anyway as well. Coms, communication radios I mean, sorry, that was always denied to bring that in.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you've alluded to this already, and this may be an obvious question, but once the list was approved by the VRS, by what means of transport would the supplies eventually be taken to the DutchBat base?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: By trucks, Dutch trucks, through a route to -- towards the enclave. And it came from the area of Tuzla or the area of Sarajevo. That's where they started from anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how would you become aware that a convoy had actually been approved and was scheduled?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Again by fax from my logistic base. They informed me that. And then a convoy would apply with the exact contents of that convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Would you describe for the Trial Chamber, sir, the process by which the convoys physically reached the battalion?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, they drove down the road but were -- well, I don't know exactly how many times but checked by Bosnian Serb check-points. They had to step out, identify themselves, and the load of the trucks was checked, and then exactly according to the lists they had to carry. And then after all these check-points they ultimately came into the enclave. The last check was on the very edge, on the confrontation line near our observation post Papa, what we called Yellow Bridge. That was the last Bosnian Serb check-point.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, would you see a final document of some sort which listed what the VRS ultimately permitted on the convoy?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. That was in fact the list that was sent to me when the convoy was planned, and they informed me that they would come down, and mostly I got a corrected list when the convoy came in ultimately, because quite a lot of things disappeared on the way down to the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And who supplied you with that corrected list, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Convoy commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And were you able to compare what --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- UNPROFOR had asked for and what the VRS had approved and arrived?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: And what actually arrived, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, was this procedure and these restrictions you've just described in place when you arrived in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. That was the procedure as I found it when I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And at some point did the restrictions on the resupply convoys by the VRS intensify?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. For instance, when my last fuel convoy came in in February.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, part of your mission, as you testified, was to facilitate the distribution of humanitarian aid within the enclave. What was the entity which had primary responsibility for the humanitarian aid there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: There was in fact two NGOs; UNHCR taking care of food and things like that, and MSF, Medecins sans Frontieres, taking care of the medical support of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And to your knowledge was the humanitarian aid coming into the enclave subject to the same process as the DutchBat resupply?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I'm sorry to do this but if you would again try to pause after -- after my question. I know it's difficult. And what was DutchBat's actual role with respect to the humanitarian aid convoys?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: In fact, secure the transport as of the confrontation line. So when they came in or appeared at OP Papa, what the entrance was to the enclave, we sent down a platoon-like unit that escorted them to the warehouse in the city of Srebrenica. Their food or whatever was brought into the warehouse by people of the opstina, the local civil -- civil authority. When it was in the warehouse, we would withdraw and that was in fact our job. Distribution and things like that were done by the UNHCR representative in coordination with the opstina people.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, without divulging any of the NGO staff members' individual identities, did anyone from UNHCR inform you as to whether or not its convoys were being subject to the same types of restrictions that you described earlier?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: In general, we hardly got any information about these UNHCR convoys. Mostly we discovered them appearing at Papa and then had to take action. I know of a convoy that was sent back by UNHCR because they had to give the Bosnian Serb check-point diesel fuel or something, and they refused that and returned. So they had more or less the same problems we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to ask you some questions about the effects that the VRS restrictions had on DutchBat's ability to carry out its mission, and let's focus first, sir, please, on the effects of the fuel shortage. How did that affect DutchBat's operability?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: The battalion needed, in fact, 8 to 9.000 litres fuel a day to do its job. As the supplies diminished we ended, with a daily ration of 250 litres, which meant that we were not able to do our full patrolling. We had to do it by foot, which meant, the fuel lack, that we were not able to heat. We had to chop wood. We were not able to have our medical dressing station as it's called, it's some kind of a hospital, to keep that operational. We were not able to purify water because we had to do that with something that needed fuel as well, a device. We didn't have any electricity, and in the end we were hardly able to, as far as food was present, to prepare that because we couldn't cook it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to turn your attention to the effects of the VRS restriction on resupply on your weapons and weapons systems, sir. You've already testified that in new weapons or ammunition, spare parts, weapons-related testing equipment, for example, were permitted into the enclave. But what was the effect on the systems themselves that you had there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: For instance, my -- sorry. My anti-tank systems, TOW, well, I won't explain that but that's the name of the machine, needed a periodical test, otherwise you can't use it. That needed test equipment. We couldn't get it. The rockets for my anti-tack systems, TOW and Dragon, et cetera, were ready to use in the OPs, which meant that they were -- they ran back in quality as far as that they were not usable anymore by -- by moist -- by, yeah, moisture, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: The ammunition for my mortars, without getting technical, but a mortar need for a certain distance extra loads. That's some kind of a pocket you do around it. Again, that powder was all moistured. So they couldn't be used anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you have an estimate of what percentage of the ammunition that you had with respect to the mortars, for example, was usable?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. I had about 15 per cent anyway of the mortar ammunition I should have, and of that 15 per cent up to three-quarters was not usable anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You mentioned the TOW system. Is that a missile system of some sort?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. It's a thread-guided missile system for anti-tank purposes. Reaches about 4 Ks.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did those missiles have a longevity themselves?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Sorry, longevity?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did they have an expiration date?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: How long did they last typically under normal circumstances?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Under normal circumstances not being, well, yeah, keeping ready for use, we swap them normally every four weeks. Under these circumstances, it proved that they didn't last longer than about six weeks on an OP, so we had to swap them for storage which we did not have. So the operational readiness of these systems was zero.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, in terms of, for example, small -- small arm ammunition, do you recall what percentage of required ammunition you had by, say, July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah, well, the -- the average supplies ammo was 16 per cent, and I remember that for small arms ammunition we were up to 30 per cent of the supply of the amount we needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall exactly how old some of your ammunition was, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, yeah, that was brought in 1994 with the first battalion and never changed later on. And then again, just for your understanding, in normal circumstances when we are operational, ready, we swap even the small calibre ammunition every ten days because it goes back in quality being in -- in the rifles, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, how about with respect to the DutchBat troop rotations, sir? Were there restrictions placed on DutchBat's ability to rotate its soldiers in and out?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah, well, we could say till the end of March or April that was -- there were problems with those convoys, personnel convoys, but that was more teasing than operational danger, in fact, but as of April it was finished and we had had quite a lot of guys out who couldn't come in anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: When you arrived in January of 1995, what was the fighting strength, to use I guess that term, of your combat-trained soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: About 300. To be exact, I believe 318.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And after the VRS restrictions kicked in, sir, you mentioned that you had a lot of soldiers who couldn't come in anymore. What were you down to?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: In the end we had 147.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And during this -- this time when you were experiencing these restrictions, did you have a term that you used within the battalion for what was going on?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. We called that convoy terror.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to turn your attention now, sir, to a new area. You testified a few moments ago about an increase in firing incidents from Serb forces on DutchBat patrols and -- and positions. Did that in combination with other things prompt some discussions with the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina regarding a -- an idea of how to defend the enclave?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. We had a -- I personally had that discussion with the Chief of Staff of the 28th Division. Problem was, of course, as we were UN troops and as being UN impartial, but it was absolutely impossible to -- to give any substance to the deterrence we had to do when only my observation posts should -- in case that there was a Serb attack should try to defend things or to prevent the Serbs coming in. So we had a strange discussion about how that would look like, which went like, well, question of the Chief of Staff 28th was: What will UNPROFOR do as soon as the -- the Serbs will attack the enclave? And under the -- my orders I was only able and authorised to defend my own observation posts. So we came to a -- an understanding that when I defended my observation posts and the Bosnian army, so the Muslims, would defend the area in between, without integrating the observation posts I would be still that UN impartial force, and they would cover the areas between the observation post, and we had some coordinated defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Was an element of these discussions or was one of your considerations during these discussions the actual security of your own forces in those observation posts should there be an attack, specifically with respect to knowing what the Muslim forces would be up to?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Sorry. The point is that -- that security of my own troops is not a big issue. The point was that we -- it is impossible when there is an attack and there are two parties and even three parties operating in an area that two parties do not exactly cooperate but have more or less the same aim, which is prevent the other party to come into the enclave. You can't do that without any coordination on the spot. For instance, when there were Muslim forces next to an observation post and they would leave without telling us, I had a major problem because my observation post would be out in the Bosnian Serb area alone and surrounded. I think that answers your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Was there -- and I think you just alluded to this, but was there something about the very nature of the OPs themselves which required this type of discussion, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: The problem was that giving -- following the order to deter by presence the locations of the observation posts were military seen absolutely ridiculous 6. We're on top of hills. We even had to put lights on them by night to show that we were still there. They were painted white, so we were absolute sitting ducks if anything went wrong. And if you -- to that comes a non-coordinated operations of a third party, being the Bosnian Muslim army, then it's ridiculous to start defending anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to turn your attention, sir, to the VRS attack on OP Echo.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall the date that that attack occurred?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Beginning of June, 3rd of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Would you please just briefly describe for the Trial Chamber what happened.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: We got report through Bravo Company, the company was responsible for that area that there was some movement in front of OP Echo. The movement proved to be Serb infantry. Then the Serb infantry yelled -- used a loudspeaker to tell the OP that they had to go, they had to withdraw because the Serbs wanted to come in. B Company asked me permission to do that. I denied that. And then they came under attack and in the end the Serbs took Echo over, and the crew withdrew in the very last moment with my authorisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you mentioned an attack, what did the attack on the OP consist of, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: There was about 40 infantry supported by a tank at Tango five fighters, the main battle tank, and a gun on the edge, ridge at Zeleni Jadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And were there actually shots fired during the attack, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what -- was there damage to the OP?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, the tower was hit. The observation tower was hit by firing -- the firing main battle tank and the area was fired at by the gun; it was an anti-aircraft gun standing up there. But was used to support the Serb attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Following the attack, did you take any steps to replace in some form OP Echo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. I ordered B Company to send two armoured -- two APCs each to -- to block the -- the approach to the city of Srebrenica, which meant in northern direction, and to block the approach in the Swedish Shelter Project. South of the enclave there was a new built village of barracks and there were about 3.000 fugitives in there, and having the area to Echo the access to both areas was open for the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You just referred to 300 fugitives.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Sorry. Sorry, it must be 3.000 fugitives.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you say "fugitives," what are you referring to, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, people that probably in 1993 or something came to that area but were not real locals, so Muslim fugitives from the area around the enclave who came to that area and were -- were housed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think this would be a good time, Madam Usher, if we could show map 6, or somebody with e-court knowledge. It's number 2111. And if we could shift the image up a little bit, please. Just a little bit more. That's great. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, do you have an image in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you just describe just generally what this depicts?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: In fact, you see the surroundings of the -- of the enclave, and the dots with letters to it are our observation posts. Referring to what I said blocking the Serb approach, after the possible Serb approach, after Echo was taken that resulted in the establishment of the observation posts Uniform and Sierra. And Sierra is on the approach to what I call the Swedish Shelter Project. And Uniform was on the higher ground just on the approach in the direction of to the city of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And those OPs, as you've described them, are located to the south, south-east of the enclave as depicted on this map; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And they are marked with an E, U and an S moving from right to left, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah, that is correct. Still the old trait that I call it Sierra and Uniform, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's right. Now, you've alluded to this somewhat, sir, but why was this a militarily significant location?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, OP Echo was exactly on the road that went east-west. You can see that on the map. The road that goes along what is called here Zeleni Jadar. It's an important connection east-west, and there was just the small edge you see on the map, the small corner. It was within the Bosnian enclave, so they couldn't use that road. There was a significant mining area, but again their connections from east to west was quite impossible there not having that road, and we thought that purpose of the attack was to get control over that road and the possibility to use it to the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what, if any, were the concerns that you referred to earlier with respect to that Swedish Shelter Project?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, there were 3.000 civilians over there, refugees, and we saw -- we thought that they could be jeopardised, or there was a substantial danger for them when the Bosnian Serb army could move in that area without any problem, not stopped. That's why I ordered them to go to S and U, as you say it, and block these approaches.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, did the increase in close firing by the VRS, the attack on OP Echo and your perceived vulnerability of the Swedish Shelter Project, did that prompt a specific communication by Colonel Karremans to higher command that you recall, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: I know that Colonel Karremans then made a -- quite a large commander assessment of the situation and indicating -- well, not indicating, but making very clear that it was a very critical situation. Not only the fact that a part of the enclave was taken by the Serbs but the situation of the battalion and the civilian population as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And again you've testified to some degree to this and I'm not asking for a lot of detail, but did the elimination of OP Echo prompt internal discussions in DutchBat about what that action might have meant in terms of the VRS's larger intentions with respect to the enclave?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, in the beginning I thought that it was the beginning of a major attack on the enclave, but when they didn't proceed in northern direction and my own troops were able to get that far south as S and U indicate, I -- in the beginning we did not understand what was going on because it's -- obviously it was not major attack, because normally when you do an attack you have success, you keep up the momentum, you keep on rolling, because that keeps your opponent out of equilibrity. Then we concluded that it was a more a less a test case, and the main effort was done just to get control of that road I described before.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, the Trial Chamber has already heard testimony concerning the VRS attack on the enclave so I won't go through an hour by hour account of what happened, but I would like to take you essentially through a chronological review of some main events and recollections that you have of -- of the events that occurred following the attack. Where were you when the VRS assault on the enclave began on July 6th?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: In the operations room.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you describe the reports that you were getting with respect to where the main effort of the attack was concentrated?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah, well, in fact it started around the 6th of July with heavy firing in the area of the observation post Foxtrot, F, if you want. That increased, was direct firing on the observation post, but there was more shelling in the other area as well, but the main effort was obviously in the area of OP Foxtrot, F.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we no longer have map 6 on the screen and I won't ask that it be brought back up at the -- oh, is it still there? Oh, okay, great. Would you just point out, please, where OP Foxtrot is?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: It's the area that I described before, that is at the eastern -- south-eastern border of the -- of the enclave. You see the dot with the letter F. In combination with U and S, we had the Serb penetration at least under observation, and the massive or the main effort of the Serb actions were in the -- directly in the area of F, observation post Foxtrot on the south-eastern part of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And Foxtrot is due north of Echo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Usher. We won't need it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you receive reports that the town of Srebrenica was being shelled?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. B Company reported random shelling of the city, and there was some shelling of -- of the position at the southern edge of the city already.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how about the Charlie Company or the main compound in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. Well, there was firing at the UN base at Potocari and the direct surroundings. But again, it was obvious it was an absolutely massive firing in the area of Foxtrot.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you begin to receive reports of civilian casualties in Srebrenica town and elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Reports of B Company who saw that civilians were brought into the civil hospital in Srebrenica, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did DutchBat assist in bringing in those wounded?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. We had our armoured ambulances, I should say, or missed the word, but you know what I mean. When we were around, we brought the people to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you describe what types of fire OP Foxtrot received in?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: All kinds, small calibre machine-gun, tank fire and mortar.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Was there a standing order covering what DutchBat soldiers manning the OPs were to do if directly attacked?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. The order to the OPs was defend the OP. And the order to the company commanders were that the -- was in fact that they didn't have to ask for withdrawal before the BiH withdrew.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm just looking at the transcript and the answer that the transcript indicates is that the order was to defend the OP and the order to the company commanders was the fact they didn't have to ask for withdrawal before the BiH withdrew. Can you just amplify what that means a little bit, sir, please?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you can't say an OP commander -- a commander of an observation post that he can destine himself when he is to withdraw from an OP. But seeing the positions -- I must be careful that I won't give here some tactical detail story, but seeing the locations of the observation posts and the easy way that the opponent can get quite close to the observation post, it means that the reaction time to withdraw is very shortly, if you want to. You can't give that to the judgement of the local sergeant, NCO. The company commander must decide it. And there was a guideline that, well, you can ask for it what you want, but as long as the BiH is in position you will not get consent in withdrawing any OP.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. So is another way of looking at that that consent would not be granted to withdraw as long as the Muslim forces were there as well?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, your previous answer raises a related question I wanted to ask you. The -- it's fair to say that once the attack began in earnest on July 6th that events started moving very rapidly in terms of decisions that DutchBat had to make. Is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, can you describe just generally how the command decision-making changed, if at all, during the course of the subsequent events?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: To make it clear I'll have to enlighten something, you already -- we already discussed the fact that quite a lot of our personnel was still in Zagreb, couldn't return to the enclave. Normally a battalion staff has an S3. That's the operations officer. He in fact is doing the tactical part of commanding the battalion when under fire. But luckily the S3 was in Zagreb as well. In fact, I was the only staff officer rested. So coordination within the battalion staff was easy, which meant that the -- the colonel was called to the phone any time by a general from anywhere, and the fact that -- and I was in the operations room so that tactical decisions within the guidelines of the colonel, I did that because you have to be quick. It's all split-second work.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to take you now to the 8th of July. This is the day that Private Van Renssen was killed. Do you recall OP Foxtrot finally falling that day, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah, well, already told that there was increased firing at the OP. It was hit several times. The defence wall was blown away by the tank fire, so they asked permission to withdraw. I gave that because the BiH was not inside anymore. They didn't inform us they were gone but they were gone. Then they waited for a pause in firing to withdraw but it was too late. They were run over by Serb forces, but were allowed to withdraw to Srebrenica. About 700 metres away from -- from -- on that route to Srebrenica they were stopped by a Bosnian -- a BiH position, a position of the 28th Division. The commander -- they wouldn't let them through, so the commander checked with his company commander, went under armour, as we call it, or had to, and tried to cross that -- that -- that -- what would you call it, that blockade, in fact. They had some stuff on the road. During that, one of the BiH soldiers fired at the APC and hit the gunner who was not under armour yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we may be a couple minutes early, but I think this probably would be a good time to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Everything seems to be in place and everyone also. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Before we get going again, sir, I've been implored to continue to speak slowly and to create as much of a pause between my questions and the answers as possible. So we'll keep trying.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: I'll keep on doing my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's difficult. I acknowledge that. We fall in the same trap ourselves. But your cooperation, of course, is solicited.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, we left off with the fall of OP Foxtrot on 8 July. I'd like to take you now to 9 July. Do you recall receiving reports about what was going on with the remaining OPs? And let's focus on OP Mike and then OPs Sierra and Uniform, taking Mike first, please.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: OP Mike is on the northern border of the enclave, and there were reports that Mike was under fire as well, mortar fire and direct firing. Through the commander of C Company, he asked me permission to withdraw a couple of hundred metres to avoid that firing. It was granted, and as far as I recollect he took a position on the edge of the village of Jaglici. Then Sierra, Uniform, well, the Serbs started then what we called Pacmanning the OPs. Pacman, that little game snatching things away. I don't know whether Sierra and Uniform fell on the 9th exactly which one did on what day. Sorry. What was reported in the beginning of the -- out of that area was that there was on the 9th a continuing battle in that area between probably Bosnian BiH forces and the Serb forces, and Uniform was under fire as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you receive information, in fact, that the Swedish shelter refugees had indeed begun to move?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: As I said, I don't recollect whether that was the 9th or 10th, but Sierra fell, was taken over by the VRS, and then I ordered B Company to send in another APC who again tried to block the approach in the direction of the Swedish Shelter Project. That APC had to go through a western approach, and then in the woods he encountered pretty -- many people, civilians, sheltering there, and they concluded that that was the population of Swedish Shelter Project. Part of those civilians was in the direction of the city of Srebrenica, but I don't know whether they all arrived in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, on 9 July, do you recall receiving any instructions, orders, or guidelines from UNPROFOR higher command?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. We were ordered to defend the city of Srebrenica by -- with all our military means.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you translate that order into a subsequent order to your forces?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. I wrote an operational order to B Company ordering him to take blocking positions generally on the south edge of the -- of the city of Srebrenica. We reinforced him with a couple of APC, what we call the QRF, Quick Reaction Forces of the other company. So we tried to give him the means to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what was the purpose of those blocking positions, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Purpose of these positions were literally to defend Srebrenica, which means to prevent the Serbs to enter the city of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I want to show you with the assistance of Madam Usher a document that we only came across recently. The Defence has been provided a copy with a translation. It doesn't have a 65 ter number or a court number as yet, so I'll just place it on the ELMO if we could. I have copies of this document as well as the English translation for the Court should the Court desire to have a hard copy to look at as Colonel Franken is reading the Dutch original and translating simultaneously. Sir, do you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Thayer. Let me see if we get agreement on this. What we see on the ELMO is the -- this document in Dutch, which with the exception of the witness himself very few of us would understand. I think what is more important is that we now can follow in -- in English. So if there is a translated copy of it, I suggest we substitute what we have on the ELMO with the English version. The accused will be able to follow when refers -- specific reference is made to parts of this document. In the meantime, the witness may retain the copy in whichever language he prefers. Certainly he should have the Dutch original of the document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you for that guidance, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, do you have the Dutch in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And -- and I see that we have the first page of the English translation on the screen. The English translation version, sir, where can you -- can you say who this memo is from and whom it is to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How many of these, do you have just one copy? One copy. So what I suggest is -- one moment, Mr. Thayer. I apologise to you for interrupting you. But I what I suggest, Madam Usher, is that you hand this to Mr. Popovic, and he will -- you will go through it very quickly before we proceed with the questions so that you will know what kind of a document we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've handed one to General Gvero. No doubt he can share with Mr. Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. And do any of the Defence team need a copy of the document in B/C/S apart from English? Or do you have both already? Yeah, they have both already. Let's proceed, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, you have a copy of a Dutch document in front of you. Do you recognise what that is?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. That is the order I gave to the commander of B Company, Captain Groen, concerning the defence of the city of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Moving the document up a little bit. Thank you. The first paragraph that is headed "Task," can you just summarise what that -- the bulk of that paragraph is meant to communicate?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. In fact, what he has to do where, in what position. It says that he has to prepare and here -- it says here "further organise," but the Dutch text is in fact "establish a defence in the southern border of Srebrenica." And I'm giving his left and -- or his west and his eastern border which means that within that area you should do your job. And the note is: "This is a seriously meant green order." That means -- in fact, we had a difference between blue operations, meaning operations within the context of the UN, and blue is referring to the colour of our equipment, blue helmets, et cetera. And the green order was specifically given to tell him that he could use immediately all his means without the restrictions of the UN to execute his order. In fact, it meant you have to proceed now as a normal army, not a UN army. That's what I meant and to make very clear to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, moving down one item under "Movements."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you describe what you were communicating here?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: In fact, we -- you can then say by means we reinforce him with means with some APCs personnel and anti-tank weapons, and the order to these means was that they had to leave the camp Potocari and such a time that they arrive in Srebrenica was at 0330 hours in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to direct your attention to the second page of the English translation, and I just note for the record that the Dutch original version is a single-page document, but turning your attention to the second page of the English translation. Can you explain, please, the meaning of the various items under "Coordinating provisions," just briefly, sir, if you would.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. I hand-picked the commander of the positions, because commander B Company had still the responsibility for all this area, and it was a specific Captain Hageman pointed out by me to be commander of those blocking positions. It says at what time, 0500 hours, all the units have to be in position. And then some remarks about the quality of -- when possible dig yourselves in, et cetera. It's some -- some guidelines, general guidelines but not -- not very important. Unless he had to count on in the English translation the word "Hrm" which means be prepared to. It's a Dutch abbreviation that they took over. He had to be prepared to be supported by close-air support.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I think that will do it with that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon. One moment, because -- okay. I think it's clear enough in the transcript. I just wanted to make sure that this "Hrm" is carefully reproduced. Close-air support would be the full version of the CAS that appears on that. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would just like to raise the Trial Chamber's attention to the fact that the document presently being used -- that was just used by the Prosecution of course is a new document. This document never appeared on the Prosecution's intended list of exhibits. It does not have a Rule 65 ter number. Normally we would object and basically say that the Prosecution before using such a document must make an application to say why this document was not presented on its list of exhibits according to Rule 65 ter. That being, Mr. President, that this document, even though it was obtained recently by the Prosecution as was mentioned, what we see here is that it appears that this document indeed already has an ERN number, that it was a document in the possession of the Prosecution, but at some point it was decided or simply they missed a document and did not include it on their list. We simply say, Mr. President, that the Prosecution should, when they come across a document like this, first make an application, explain why the document is not on their list, where the document comes from, so that at least we have some time to prepare. In this case, we were given this document yesterday. We decided not to object in order to allow for the testimony of Mr. Franken to continue today, but we want -- we have to raise this to the Trial Chamber's attention. There is a second issue, Mr. President, with respect to this document, and this will again come on a few documents. There are comments put between slashes on these documents, and this appears to have been added, and it appears on many documents, appears to be added by the translation services. For example, we have on this document, we have "QRF" as being Quick Reaction Force. And then we have some of these expansions, it's written expansions unknown. There's a difference between a translation and a guessing work as to what an abbreviation really means. The person who can tell us what the abbreviation means, sorry, is the witness or at least somebody who was aware of the document, but there should not be a guessing game in terms of trying to identify what these expansions or these abbreviations mean. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think answering your last issue I think it requires very little -- very few remarks. I think that if you have doubts as to the words between backslash, then you can -- that can be raised in cross-examination with -- with the witness. That's the first one. The second -- the first point that you raised, I understood Mr. Thayer to say that the Prosecution had come into possession of this document only recently. Are you contesting that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, the fact of the matter, Mr. President, is we received some notes from the Prosecution and I'm not sure exactly when they came across this document, because according to some information that we have this -- what is referred to in a memo that we've received from my colleague is called a green order with an ERN number. Now, in terms of this document, it talks about a Rule 70 waiver, meaning that the Prosecution already had this document but for some reason appears to have elected or chosen not to use it. Now they want to use it and they changed their mind. Now, that's a big difference between you have a document, you choose not to use it, and then suddenly with another witness comes and you say, "Oh, well, yes, I'm going to use it today." I think that's a difference. Maybe that's not the case. Maybe my colleague can explain, but that's the purpose of my intervention. If the Prosecution wants to use a new document, they should make an application and say, "We have a new document. Here's what it is. Here's where it comes from. Here is why we want to use it." And then we can argue and basically the Chamber can decide whether it should be allowed to do so or not. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Mr. Thayer, had these issues not been brought up, obviously your explanation that this document had just come to you recently would have provided the explanation why it was not included on the 65 ter list. However, the issue has been raised, and I think I have to call upon you to tender any explanation you may have.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. And my learned colleague has a fair point with respect to these two documents, actually, that we will be dealing with in the course of Colonel Franken's testimony.
