I misspoke with respect to this particular document. This document we have had. It has not been identified before, as far as I know, by anybody as existing. It was attached to the statement of another DutchBat officer. No one, as far as I know, has seen it ever, and that is -- it came into my possession very recently, and I tried to get a hold of Colonel Franken as soon as I could to see if he would waive his Rule 70 privilege with respect to it and communicate that as soon as I could. So we have had this in a collection. I don't believe anybody's actually seen this particular document, Your Honour. I came across it through a massive Rule 68 search that we are conducting as a regular part of our ongoing duties and compliance with the rules of the Trial Chamber. With respect to the second document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Stop there for the time being. That is the explanation that Mr. Thayer has for the Defence. Do you -- can we proceed, or do you wish to comment on it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President. For today with this document we can proceed. But this is a situation that needs to be brought to your attention for future documents so that we have an ongoing procedure. But I don't want to interrupt the testimony of this witness. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Next point with the other document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to this second document, this document indeed we only came into possession of on Thursday last. These are documents which we undertook efforts to recover at the request of counsel for accused Miletic, documents which were mentioned in the NIOD report which we have placed the Defence on notice of. It's been in existence for some time, but we received a specific request to search or contact NIOD for documents relating to our anticipated live trial witnesses. We have done so. We expect to receive some of those documents shortly. They will be translated as soon as possible and furnished to Defence counsel. One of those documents was translated last week and furnished to Defence counsel today. The document was received Thursday, translated Friday and Saturday, and then disclosed today. This document that I'm referring to that I will use with Colonel Franken actually has not even been translated yet. It is a document I only had an opportunity to discuss with Mr. McCloskey over the weekend. We made the decision that it had some -- some probative and relevant value, and we have undertaken to have it translated in fact as we speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you so much, Mr. Thayer. And I take it from you, Mr. Bourgon, speaking on behalf of all of the Defence teams, that we can proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I have not discussed this with my colleagues, but I believe that is the case, but I was not speaking on behalf of everybody because I did not check with them first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I apologise to you for having misunderstood that. Does any Defence team wish to disassociate itself with the position taken by Mr. Bourgon, both in relation to the first and the second document? In other words, okay, we can proceed. Yes, Mr. Thayer. And I thank the -- you for the explanations and the Defence teams for their cooperation. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just one final question, sir, with respect to these blocking positions, and forgive me if you've answered this previously but I just wanted to clarify it. How many blocking positions were there and what names were they assigned?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: There were originally planned four blocking positions. They were called Bravo 1 up to Bravo 4, and there was one planned position for my forward air controllers, which means that is a team that is able to lead planes on -- attacking planes on a target.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, do you recall approximately when your blocking positions actually were established?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Because they had problems by taking their positions. It was prevented by a Serb fire. It was at about 0630 that morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And this would be the morning of 10 July --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, let's just take up where you -- where you left off there. What reports did you receive concerning fire received by DutchBat positions and personnel, and let's begin with those blocking positions.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, the commander, Captain Hageman, who had a central position, I recollect it as being Bravo 2, was not able to reach that because he came under fire of a Serb T 55 main battle tank, was shot off the road with his APC, had to withdraw. That position was adjusted. The position on the west side, Bravo 1, had to change his position because he was under fire of Serb tanks and Serb artillery. Bravo 4 in the east had no problems originally, and Bravo 3 had to change because he was under fire by machine -- machine-guns but took reserve positions, which mean it's a position where he can do the same job just on another spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You mentioned the position of Captain Hageman taking fire and being driven off the road. Did you have to take any steps to try to recover that --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah, we tried to -- the recovery vehicles were positioned at Potocari and so I sent down one of them who came in the fire right out of the gate of Potocari by the anti-tank gun that was positioned in the area of OP P, Papa. But again when he tried to go to the vehicle of Captain Hageman he came under fire of that came Tango 55 main battle tank and had to withdraw, so we didn't succeed in recovering that vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you receive any reports of injuries suffered by DutchBat soldiers or crew members?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. There were a couple of shrapnel wounds, light injuries, but they could stay in position and could keep on working or doing their job.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And were those injuries sustained by blocking position crew members, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Bravo 1 and the western position, they had three or four wounded by shrapnels, and some of the crew of -- the gunner of Captain Hageman had some injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now I'd like to focus your attention for a moment to Bravo Company and that area.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What reports were you receiving on 10 July concerning the attack on -- on that area, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, as I told you, my blocking positions were under fire, and there was a massive shelling of the city of Srebrenica, including our compound. There were reports of wounded, but we didn't count them because they were taken to the civil hospital and we had our hands full in doing other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you at some point request a count of the number of detonations or -- or artillery explosions on that day, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Standard procedure was that when there was shelling that -- that the patrol or the observer reported the amount and the -- if known, the weapon system that was firing. B Company did that on the 10th as well, but I ordered them to stop when they came up to 160 or 200 or something like that. It was no use anymore to report that, just filling paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And by this time, sir, were you able to identify and count the VRS artillery or firing positions?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. We already knew of -- of about 16 positions, but then we came to a count of about 32 artillery or mortar positions active. We got reports of about six different main battle tanks operational.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, at some point on 10 July, do you recall DutchBat receiving an ultimatum from the VRS?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: On the 10th, you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, on or about the 10th.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, as far as I recollect, UN sent an ultimatum to -- to the -- the Serbs, the Bosnian Serbs, and they reacted with an ultimatum to DutchBat, in fact, saying, okay, stop your hostile activity and with an arrangement that we could leave through Papa, the -- in an order with the civil population, leave the enclave, and they demanded that we left our equipment and weapons, et cetera, as far as I recollect it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to show you a document. And for the record, this is the second document that I described previously that has just come into our possession. And with the assistance of Madam Usher, I'd just like to place it on the ELMO. Sir, you have a document in Dutch in front of you. I'd just ask you to take a moment and read it. And again, we are in the process of getting this document translated, so for the time being, with the Trial Chamber's permission, I'd just ask you to translate into English directly from this document. And when you do so, sir, it's even more important to pause to do so, because it's particularly important for the accused to be able to understand what you're saying. Now, having seen in document, can you describe what it is?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: In fact, it is a written version of the -- of the radio message we got from the BSA and I tried to describe the details but I see the details here, and it concerns the information of commander B Company, because the other commanders were in the area of the HQ because I -- so I could do that verbally, but Captain Groen was in Srebrenica, so I sent this down to him, and it concerned that ultimatum of what we call the Bosnian Serb army. Text was: "The UN is not disarming the Muslims so we will do that, and as 11th of July, 0600 hours till 48 hours later, civilians, soldiers of the BiH, DutchBat can give -- hand in their weapons and leave the enclave through Yellow Bridge." Yellow Bridge is the Bosnian Serb check-point at the north part of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let me just stop you right there.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: I'm going too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, no, no, you're fine. I just want to clarify something. This particular paragraph, there's a word that precedes the colon on the line that has the BSA on it. It's "betreft." What is that word?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: B-e-t -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It's -- right next to where it says "ultimatum BSA."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: There is a word directly to the left of that.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Oh, "betreft." That's a Dutch word, means concerned. This concerns the ultimatum of the BSA. That's literally translated what the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now I'm sorry, I interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You were about to talk about the last line of that section.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. "NGOs, UNHCR, et cetera, can leave immediately through Yellow Bridge." Again, Yellow Bridge being the Serb check-point in the north.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just raise an issue. We have just received the English translation of the document. I can place this on the ELMO and work from here on, or at the Court's pleasure we can continue with the Dutch translation via Colonel Franken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So replace that with the English version. More or less it will also give us an opportunity to control what we've just heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do have extra copies of the English translation which I can distribute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: To -- oh, thank you, Madam Usher. May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, feel free to rely on the Dutch version you have in front of you or the English translation. The bottom portion of that memorandum, would you please explain that to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, but if you allow me, I have a remark about the translation of the first part.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: It says "DutchBat can hand in weapons," as if there was a possibility not to do so. That was absolutely not the case. We had to hand in our weapons when we should have done that. Then the second part, "UN reaction," was that the Bosnian Serb army should withdraw to lines of Morillon, as was the UN border of the enclave because there were three borders. In fact, there was a BiH border, BSA border and the UN border, and that differed significantly. Every "AV," which is the Dutch abbreviation for attack. Every attack should be left behind. Or they should stop their attack it was meant. And the order was to withdraw to those Morillon lines as of 0600 on the, what is it, the 11th. That was the reaction of the UN, and this message was to inform commander B Company what was going on on that level.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I think that takes care of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What does processing mean? Top line.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Top line, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Processed 13th July.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is later on a -- a -- they say they filed it or processed it on the 13th, but that is not done by me or something. It is somebody who made this copy or whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Judge Kwon. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would just like to clarify something the witness just said about, he made a comment on the translation. I would just like to know if that was a substantive comment or whether the original says something other than "can hand in weapons."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I understood it. But Colonel -- Mr. Franken has heard your remark, and I think he can easily answer that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is significant, because in fact it's a mistake in the translation. The original message says, "You have to hand in your weapons," and the translation says, "You can," giving the possibility -- the possibility not to do so, but it's not relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And thank you, Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, that brings us now to the 11th of July. By that time were you also receiving reports concerning the fate of the remaining OPs that you had described earlier? I think the term you used for it was a Pacman video game. And what do you mean by that and was that continuing until the 11th?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: What I meant is that the OPs were one by one taken over by the Serbs. After the Foxtrot incident with which I mean the killing of one of my soldiers, we ordered the OPs only to withdraw when they got permission to withdraw, when there was some kind of an agreement with the local Muslim commander, because we were very keen to prevent more soldiers shot by -- by the Muslim army. So what I meant by Pacman, that one by one the Muslims left their positions without telling us and my OPs found themselves absolutely surrounded by the Bosnian Serb army. And during that day, and I don't know exactly which OP when fell, but it ended in that the OP Charlie and OP Alpha were still in position, and Delta was in another position a bit more north and more or less the rest of them were taken over or withdrawn, with the exception of Papa, because Papa we kept that. In the northern entrance, we kept that operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what happened to the DutchBat soldiers who had been manning those OPs as they were being overrun, captured or attacked by the VRS forces?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: In most cases they have to hand in their small calibre weapons and were taken with their APC to -- whether Bratunac. Some of them stayed some period in that mining area, that is the area directly south of the enclave, were brought to Milici, but in the end they all ended in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And based on the reports that you were receiving, were those soldiers free to leave their positions or free to leave that location in Bratunac or --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: No, no. They were -- they were POWs. They were taken prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: At some point on the 11th of July did you decide to issue any orders regarding continuing to defend the town of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct. The situation was that we had an attack on the 10th. The evening of the attack we fired upon the Serb army. They withdrew. Then we found out in the morning of the 11th that the 28th Muslim Division had disappear. Nobody was there anymore. And the population, the civilians, were moving into -- massively in the city itself over in our compound of the B Company, and then we tried to lead them in the direction of Potocari. Commander B Company had soldiers on the road who started to walk in the direction of Potocari, and they followed, which meant that defending Srebrenica, the city, an empty city, was of no use, and I gave B Company orders to withdraw at the tail of that column of refugees a northern position, in northern direction. His mission was stay between the Serbs and the civilians and bring them -- bring them north. If you come to Potocari, take position in the south on the edge of Potocari, front south, and again start blocking any Serb approach. Another reason for ordering him withdraw Srebrenica was that by that time being the 28th Muslim Division away, I had Serb infantry on the high edges already past my left and right flanks. So we were in the air and in fact, well, moved out of position.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You described the movement of the Muslim refugees together with some of your men northwards. Did you receive reports about their experience as they moved in that northerly direction?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Commander B Company, of course, informed me in detail where his positions were and how far the proceedings or the ongoing of that column was. I got reports of shelling of the column. Wounded we picked up and loaded them on the APCs and brought them to Potocari on that way. That was in fact in general the reports I got, because every detailed report is not relevant now.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you know what kind of fire the column of refugees was receiving?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, mostly mortar and artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you make any logistical preparations for the arrival of these refugees given the information you were receiving, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. I ordered base commander Major Otter to recce a route into the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let me stop you right there. What does the term "recce" mean?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: To -- what do you call that in normal English? To find out a road, a safe road, route, I should say, into the camp because the road in front of our base was in the direct site of Serb artillery and Serb tanks, and I didn't want those civilian columns moving up that road because I had reason to believe that it was -- they would be fired upon. That's what he did, and then we had a line of guides to guide the people into our camp in Potocari, and I gave my logistics people and my medics orders to prepare the receiving of the people. So make a first aid post, et cetera, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You described the -- wanting to keep the column of refugees out of the direct sight of the Serb artillery. Can you describe with a little bit more detail where you had identified those pieces being located and what they were, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: In -- in the area of the OP Papa there was a small ridge and a saddle what we call it, a lower part, and in that position was an anti-tank gun who had been firing all the time at the -- our base. Directly east of it there was a position of a T55, a main battle tank, and further north there were positions of MRS -- what is it? Multiple launch rocket systems.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: At this time if we could have P01516 displayed on e-court, please. And this is the one we need upside down, please. Actually, if we could zoom out just a bit, please. Just a little bit more. Zoom out. I'm sorry. Perfect. Okay. Sir, do you have an image on your screen?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'll just ask you to take a moment and orient yourself and ask you if you can recognise what this is?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: In fact, that's an aerial photograph of -- of the location of our HQ in Potocari and the -- a part of the village of Potocari itself. The way -- the road you see north-south going is the road between Bratunac and Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And I'll ask you some more specific questions about some of the landmarks and features. But basically are you able to make out various landmarks and structures on this document based on your experience there, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to ask you to -- with the assistance of Madam Usher to take a stylus and show you how to do it. It's a lesson in time travel. Okay. I'd ask you if you could just write "UN base" to the right of the actual compound if you can identify it there on the -- and just draw an arrow pointing to it, please.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you see an area that you knew as the Ekspres bus compound or the bus company?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And would you please write "bus compound" to the right of it and an arrow, please.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you see the general area of the abandoned factories that have been referred to, and if you do, could you just please write "factories" to the left of it and an arrow pointing to that area, please.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you -- can you make out a feature that you knew as the "White House" on this overview, sir, and if you --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If you can, would you please just write "White House" to the left and an arrow point to go it.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just for the record, the northern -- northern direction is going up on the page and south down; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Would you mark as best as you can recall the route that Major Otter had established for the reception of the refugees.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. And I'm not sure whether that was in between these buildings or the western part of these buildings I'm not sure as well. But in general, we came from the south side and we made a hole in the fence indicated there as a sign where they came in.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And where in the UN base were they physically sheltered, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: In a big factory building in the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if you'd just place an X on top of that, please.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if you could write your initials and date the document, please.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I think we're ready to --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you will tender that at a later stage. Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think we are done for the moment with this document. If it's saved, we can cross our fingers and let it go. Thank you, Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: How did you determine, sir, when the compound was -- was too full for your purposes?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Having experienced the situation in Srebrenica with our freedom of movement with military means when all these people were around, which was not, I had to guarantee that on the compound, being the last UN area in the enclave, I still was able to move with my military means, my APCs, if necessary. And secondly, I didn't want the refugees to be exposed to the views of the Bosnian Serb army, especially not directly in the line of fire of the artillery and tanks I described to you before. So that's why I decided to use that building. In fact, it's the only one that gave that cover anyway. And when it was full to closed down, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And where were the refugees directed after that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, they stayed more or less in the area of the bus station, the factories in the area, and on the other side, on the western side of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Which you have marked on your --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Before, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- previous document. Okay. I want to turn your attention, sir, briefly to another event on the afternoon of 11 July. At some point was close-air support finally delivered?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you receive any response from the VRS to that close-air support?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. Must have been around 1400 hours when the close-air support was a fact. I got through the communication means of one of the -- let's say of my APCs standing in Bratunac, the APCs that came with the OP crews to that POW site, I got an English message read by one of my NCOs, my NCOs, which said that close-air support had to stop immediately or BSA would shell to the ultimate the area of our base, including the locations where the refugees were, and they would kill my soldiers, being POW.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, let's take the latter portion of that message first, sir. How seriously did you take the threat to your personnel?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. Not that serious. The only thing what in my opinion could be done is that they would use them as a shelter or as a cover for -- for -- on important locations, a sort of human shield which they did before in other parts of Bosnia. I didn't -- I didn't believe that they would really execute them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: How seriously did you take the threat to shell the HQ and the compound with the refugees in it, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Very serious, because they did that before. And with that I mean firing at the refugees with all means they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And at some point shortly after receiving this threat was there actually fire received by the base?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. Probably they -- they would make sure that we believed them, because very shortly after that there was a mortar shelling of the area of the bus station, and later -- shortly after that there was a full round of the MRS, the multiple rocket system in the area of Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did that fire cause any casualties among the refugees, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah, there were wounded, but I can't tell you how many because it was a tremendous crowd in panic, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to turn your attention for a couple of moments to an area which the Trial Chamber has received substantial evidence already so we went go through it in much detail, and I'm referring to the series of Hotel Fontana meetings between the evening of the 11th and the next morning the 12th of July. Just briefly, sir, did Colonel Karremans brief you following the first meeting?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah, following the first meeting he did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And as result of that first meeting you had to locate a representative from the Muslim population for the second meeting? Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you remember that person's name?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. Mr. Mandic was the first one that took part of that committee, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you see Mr. Mandic --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- when he returned from that second meeting? And again, I'm sorry, but if you could please leave a pause between --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- between our questions.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic came to the meeting, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what was his demeanour when you saw him after that second meeting?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah, he was very, very nervous and -- and almost panicking because, well, he felt the responsibility he was confronted with. We talked and he had the wish to speak to his government. We tried that on the evening but we couldn't reach anybody. There was a responsible minister obviously in that -- in the BiH government, but he couldn't be disturbed because he was dining. So Mr. Mandic had his problem. I tried to support him.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, did Colonel Karremans brief you after the second meeting that night?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So it's fair to say that by the evening of the 11th the refugees had already pretty much filled the compound and were crowded into the factory area and the bus area to the south --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, the mass was already present then in the night of the 11th. On the 12th, there were smaller groups still coming in, but the mass was there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And at that point what measures did you take with respect to their safety and welfare?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Their safety, we had -- I appointed a commander as a guard commander, and we had a ring of outposts around that area. Order was to prevent Serb forces or any forces to enter that -- that area. And for the welfare we had a first aid -- no, two first aid posts with medics and doctors in the area. We distributed water and some food of which we didn't have ourself very much, but that's what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I take it you spent fair amount of time in the operations room during this period; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you nonetheless make it a point to get out and about?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I thought it was important that I got out so that not only hearing the reports but seeing with my own eyes, and I -- at least twice a day I made my round outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to observe the conditions --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- of the refugees?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And would you just briefly describe how they appeared to you at that time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Totally exhausted, bad condition. In fact, lethargic. Lethargic? Yeah, that is a word. They didn't react on anything, just turned into themselves. Not prepared to help each other or whatever. We were there, and more or less they looked as if the world stopped for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Were you able to estimate approximately how many Muslim men were inside the compound and among the gathering refugees south of the compound?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Inside the compound we were pretty sure we counted them. We probably come to that; it's the well known list. And the estimations outside were around 600 up until 800 or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And as you said, we'll get to the list later. But for the time being, did you have a general idea of how many Muslim men were inside the compound?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, we estimated on 300 about.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like you to turn your attention now to the next day, the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: There was an infantry attack that commenced at some point that morning. Could you just briefly describe what you observed with respect to that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. That advance was a demonstration of a basically trained unit, men in line supported by a main battle tank and coming alongside the road from northern direction in the direction of Potocari. So from the area of OP Papa general Bratunac. Well dressed, I mean in proper uniforms. All the same uniforms. There was obviously a communication between the tank crew and the infantry outside. So more or less a demo, a demonstration of a normal army.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Where was Colonel Karremans at this time, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: He was on his way or already present at the third meeting with Mladic, and that was in Bratunac in that hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So the attack that you witnessed occurred sometime in the early morning of -- of the 12th?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Quarter past 10.00, half past 10.00, something like that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Not early for a military man?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: No, not.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you a bit later that morning have direct contact with some of those VRS forces after they entered Potocari?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Personally, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah, well, later on when Colonel Karremans returned from his meeting with Mladic, and he was trying to debrief me. Later on I had contact to a Colonel Acamovic, who was a G4 officer, he said, from Pale and who was in charge of what we called -- or what one called then the evacuation of the civil population.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just interrupt you right there, sir. I want to go back a little bit before we talk about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before we go back, if he could repeat the name because it doesn't show up in the transcript. I think it's important. Colonel who?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I recollect, Acamovic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Before we discuss the higher level Serb officers whom you encountered, did you encounter a group of other VRS soldiers somewhere in the vicinity of the compound, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. I got a report that a couple of Serb soldiers wanted to enter the compound not through the main gate but an unused gate they wanted to go in. Major Rutten reported that to me. As for orders, I went over there myself and forbid that. The only thing I -- to prevent a fighting over there quite close to the refugees. I permitted them to come in with two guys and to check whether or not, as they declared, parts of the 28th Division were in our compound. So I escorted them with four or five soldiers -- of my soldiers and they were in the compound for about four minutes and then out again.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall the appearance of these soldiers, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. Generally they were -- they were wearing all kinds of uniforms. There were a couple of them in dark uniforms, soldiers with dogs, and on my request somebody stepped forward. There was one soldier who spoke English stepped forward and declared himself the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did these soldiers all appear to be from the same unit?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Or did they appear to you to be from different units at that --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: From different units. Yeah, well, at least they didn't wear all the same uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, let's pick up where you began to answer previously. Did Colonel Karremans return at some point from that meeting in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. If you want a time it would be somewhere shortly after 12.00, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did he brief you about what happened at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, he started briefing, I should say, because he couldn't finish that because him briefing me, I got the report that there were hell of a lot of buses and trucks appearing from the -- from the north. So he stopped his briefing and I started arranging things, at least tried.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And was it at that point that you had contact with this VRS officer Acamovic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That was later on. It was later on. I suppose it's about 2.00 or 3.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Why don't we discuss for a moment your encounter with this Colonel Acamovic, sir.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did just describe who he told you he was, what he did, and what he was doing there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: It was a very short meeting, I should say. He came forward to me and said he was a colonel in the Bosnian Serb army and he was a G4 officer and responsible for the evacuation of the civilians and asked for support and specifically transport and diesel.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what was your --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what was your response to that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: I could hardly stop my laughing because they were very well aware of the fact that I did not have diesel and I refused that support.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you meet any other higher-level Serb officers that day who appeared to be involved to some degree in this whole process?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: It must be the same day that I met a Colonel Jankovic, and he said to be a colonel from Pale as well, and his mission was to prepare and -- and to coordinate the withdrawal of DutchBat out of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, given that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Thayer. Previously on -- he was asked and he answered the question relating to what kind of uniforms, whether they were wearing the same uniform. I'm referring to the small group that were allowed to enter. Did he notice any insignia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not, sir. There were some badges on these parts of uniforms, but -- but I don't really recollect them. Yeah, they looked like militia. One had camouflage trousers on, the other a jacket, et cetera. It was a complete mix of civil and military parts on their bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, given that as you testified, sir, the buses had already arrived, what did you decide to do?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, it was obvious that we want to have some control over the operation, so I -- the first buses already tried or started to leave, and I sent down, I picked out two officers in my neighbourhood, put them in the jeep and gave them the word to stay with that convoy whatever happens, and then I gave order to one of my officers, Captain Melchers, to organise a convoy escort which meant one jeep with an NCO or officer and a driver in front of that convoy and one at the tail of the convoy. And he started arranging that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just going back a moment, sir. The first two officers whom you mentioned, do you recall their names?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. Major Boering, my S5, and Captain Voerman. He was normally my personnel officer. But they happened to be at hand so I ordered them to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you attempt to stay abreast of the progress of those first convoys, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, we did. I could not get any communications with my escort team, but I heard afterwards what happened to that convoy that went well I got reports from the Pakistani battalion being in the area of Kladanj, being a UN unit. On my question whether there were people coming in, specifically men and women, they confirmed that. And later on I got reports from my escort teams as long as they were operational.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, along those lines, sir, did you start receiving reports concerning the DutchBat escorts of subsequent convoys?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: It was the first -- I mean, I believe the second convoy all went well but then there came a massive harassment of my escort teams. They were stopped, sometimes with the argument that the Serb troops that responsible for their security and it was too dangerous to drive on. So they were stopped and not allowed to drive on but the buses went on. And that varied until stopping under the threat of weapons robbed and some of my patrols came back in their underwear walking out of Serb area and every variation in between that happened, which meant I didn't get any reports, so -- so to say. My ears and my eyes were cut off.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You described the escorts being robbed. What were they robbed of, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, anything. Their vehicles, their weapons, their flak jackets, ammo, equipment in the jeep, of course. There were variations. There were escort teams who were allowed to stay in place, kept their weapons, nothing wrong, but it went down to two of my patrols coming back literally in their underpants and the rest was stolen.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, when you learned that the weapons were being stolen, what did you do in response to that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: I ordered the escort teams to go without weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how many vehicles were seized during the course of these events?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah, about 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you testified about the variation in -- in the treatment received by the DutchBat soldiers from the Serb forces. Based on the reports you were receiving, was there anything consistent or constant about what you were learning was going on with respect to your efforts to escort those convoys?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, in fact it started more or less on one moment, so my conclusion was that it was organised. It was ordered, and the reason for that for me was they -- they don't want us to be around these convoys. They don't want us to be witness of whatever happens. They want us out of the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let me diverge just for a moment. Other than the DutchBat escort vehicles which you just described, during the course of this attack and the eventual fall, what other vehicles were -- were lost to the VRS?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, quite some APCs, of course, APCs who were positioned on the OPs, and then two or three were damaged by -- by fire and were taken by the Serbs after we withdrew. Two or three jeeps again and quite a lot of small calibre weapons. But including all my POW systems, because they were positioned on the OPs, and some heavy machine-guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you register a complaint with any of the VRS officers whom you encountered, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I complained to Colonel Jankovic, and he would -- he said he would take care of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, did he take any action?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: No. I don't know whether he took any action, but I couldn't see any result.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you begin receiving reports at some point that the men were being separated from the refugees?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Separation of men was from the very beginning, of course. Mladic announced that as well. So from the very start of the evacuation men were more or less separated. The first convoy went away with men, but then probably on the Serb side it was better organised and men were taken out directly after they left the perimeter we secured.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you become aware of where some of these men were taken, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: They were brought to the "White House" building, about 150 metres out in front of our main gate, and were interrogated there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And is that the "White House" you identified on the document you previously marked, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you personally observe men at the "White House" at about --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: I've seen that they were brought there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you observe anything outside that "White House"?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. But that was not directly in the beginning. The men had to leave their probably personal belongings that were piled, let's say, about 30, 40 metres from the "White House" alongside the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Later on during this process, sir, did you learn about men who had been permitted to pass through but had been later separated?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, I never had an actual report of my own men. This is what I heard when I was back in Holland.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: When you received information about the men at the "White House" did you take any action with respect --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. We had an UNMO team, military observers of the UN, a [indiscernible] team. They were on the compound, and I sent them down there to monitor what was happening there, and the reports I got in the beginning, well, that they're -- that many men going in, exact same number men coming out, and the report that they were brought by a specific bus, a light blue bus. They were transported in the direction of the Bratunac in the beginning, at the end of every convoy and later on apart. I mean, the bus drove along, not in the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's stay on this issue of the -- of the blue buses or the blue bus. Did you personally observe the -- any of the men being placed and transported in the blue bus?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And was this occurring throughout the day on the 12th --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: -- and on the 13th, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you describe in a little bit more detail what measures you took to monitor that blue bus and the success that the monitoring met with?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. We gave order to -- one of the convoy jeeps, the escort jeeps to -- to escort specifically that bus, and the measure of success was nil because the escort was whether stopped at Papa and if he tried to drive on he was blocked by a tank or by men, so in always they tried to separate that escort jeep from that blue bus. And if he was held up in the area of Bratunac and he later on came to the tail of the convoy, the blue bus was vanished.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, let's go back to the men in the "White House" for a little bit, sir. Did you at some point receive reports that they were not being properly treated?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. The -- in the course of the 12th I got reports that they were badly treated. I sent down patrols of my own men over there in course of the afternoon. They were blocked by -- by far outnumbering Serb forces which did not allow them to go to the "White House."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And again did you speak or register a complaint with any of the VRS officers about these --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- reports?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: I again said that to Colonel Jankovic, who said that they were POWs, and if there was a -- too rude action he would take action to prevent that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did he take any action?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Again, I don't know whether he took action, but I didn't see a result. And he confirmed in fact that he had nothing to do with that because he was only there for the withdrawal of DutchBat. That was in fact the answer I got always from Colonel Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, believe we have -- is it five more minutes until the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Six.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Six. I think this would probably be a logical time in terms of the examination in time to take a break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will take a 30-minute break. We need to discuss a few things [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Thayer, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, as you've been testifying, you were monitoring the progress of the convoys, the status of the men who were being kept at the "White House" and transported. Did you begin to have concerns about the male refugees?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, because the reports made clear to me that the treatment of the men was decreasing, was getting worse. There were all kind of rumours, and somewhere around there there was a report of yelling and things like that from the "White House," et cetera. So I tried to figure out a way to protect these men a bit more than we did at the very moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you testified you'd already tried to send your own soldiers down there and that met with no --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So what did you decide to do when other measures had failed?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, in fact I tried to imitate a trick what was done before, getting the unknown people, giving them a face and a name. So I registered -- I tried to register all the men within our UN area.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what was your ultimate intention with this registration?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. Send them to higher echelons, including Holland here, the General Staff here in Holland, and request them to make it public, to mobilise the public by telling them exactly who it was, the names, et cetera, et cetera, et cetera, and hoping that it would work better than there was some unknown mass of men nobody had a name with or any identity with.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And could you just describe for the Trial Chamber briefly how this registration took place?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. I spoke about that with the committee I mentioned before, Mr. Mandic, et cetera, and asked them whether they would take care of the registration and explain the purpose I had with that registration, and they started registering the men.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now you've referred a couple of times to a committee.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Was -- was this some kind of formal group or how did this so-called committee come into being?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. One of the first, and I recollect the first meeting Colonel Karremans had with Mladic he demanded that the leaders of the enclave, military and civilian leaders, would be present at the next meeting. Problem was that the 28th Division, including their commanders and leaders and the opstina, were vanished, were disappeared, so we asked one of our interpreters whether there were in the crowd of refugees some people who could function as the representative of the refugees, and so we claimed two men and a woman who were willing to act as representative of the refugees. And that's what I call the committee. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I think you've already testified that one was Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you remember the names of the other two?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Mr. Nuhanovic, Ibrahim Nuhanovic, and a lady which name I do not recollect.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, the list that you created were you told about whether that included all of the men inside the compound?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Now, there were about 60 or 70 men who refused to be registered, and the 251 it appears later on, but 239 I thought then were willing to be registered.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you try to register the men outside the compound?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, we did that as well. But then the committee, because we were not able to do it ourself, was massively intimidated by the Serb forces to an extent that the lady had a complete nervous breakdown and had to be brought to the hospital. So they didn't have the guts anymore to go out.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: At this time I'd ask that 65 ter number 2057 be displayed on e-court, please. And if we could, please, just -- perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, do you have an image on your screen?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: I do have.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I would ask if we could just slowly scroll through the consecutive pages of the document until we reach page 10, which I believe is the last page. And if we could move the document up, please, to the bottom. Perfect. Thank you. Now, sir, having reviewed these pages do you recognise what this document is?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. That's the list I mentioned, registration of the men within the compound, and I signed it on the right side. Miscounted it but signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You've written 239. I believe you just testified it was --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And this you did at the time, sir; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that you had passed this information up your chain of command to make it public. Did you tell anyone in the VRS about this list?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. I told Colonel Jankovic that I registered the men and that the names were known not only within the UN but to the Dutch government as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you show him or any other VRS officer the list?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Why not, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Was no use of it, and then I didn't want in any way the information on this list to go directly to the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what, if anything, did you do to ensure that the list would not fall into the VRS's hands?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, I transmitted it on secure communications to Tuzla, Sarajevo, both the UN headquarters, and to The Hague here, Crisis Staff it was called in that days. And the original list I brought on my body when the battalion came out of the enclave and went to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You mentioned a moment ago Ibrahim Nuhanovic.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Other than being a member of this informal committee, as you described it, do you know whether he had any relationship to anybody in the -- in the UN compound?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. It appeared to be he was the father of one of the interpreters of the UNMOs. UNMOs, being the UN military observers.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall having a conversation with him in the evening of 12 July?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Would you please describe that conversation.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Nuhanovic came to me that he wanted to speak to me about the evacuation, so I let him in and we spoke. He wanted me to stop the evacuation, because he, as I did, feared for the fate of the men. And we had a discussion. I explained him why I could not do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what explanation did you give him?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. In fact, I told him with detailed arguments that I had to make the choice between as far as I knew about 800 up until a thousand men and 25 up to 30.000 women and children concerning their survival. I told him that I chose for the 25.000, 30.000 women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That brings us up to the 13th of July. Did the -- did the transportations resume that day?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And were they completed that day as well?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you receive any reports, either on the 12th or the 13th, that Serb soldiers had been among the refugees outside the compound during the night of 12 July?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. No. I think that were not reported to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, based on the number of soldiers you had available to guard those mass of refugees, would that have been possible?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, it would have been possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: During this same period of time, during the 12th to 13th of July, did you also receive reports of executions?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. In two cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you describe those reports for the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. First was a report of nine dead bodies in the area of the "White House" found by one of my officers. Obviously they were in a row and all shot in the back, so we concluded that there has been an execution.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Condon.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I object to this witness giving evidence of a forensic -- he's not in a position to give evidence as to the cause of death of those victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's your response to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not attempting to elicit expert information, simply what this officer related to him, what he observed, and any conclusions he drew based on those observations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have absolutely no problem in allowing the question to proceed or the witness to proceed with answering the question. Of course, you will have every opportunity to cross-examine the witness on any issue that you have referred to, if at all necessary. Yes. So I suggest you repeat your question. I can read it, actually. "Can you describe those reports for the Trial Chamber?" And, Mr. Franken, you had said, "Yes. First was a report of nine dead bodies in the area of the 'White House' found by one of my officers. Obviously they were in a row and all shot in the back, so we concluded that there had been an execution."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Any further matters that you would like to state in answering this question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, I would like to describe the second report I got about execution, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. And I heard through the colonel who reported that one of the soldiers of C Company, being a member of one of the outposts, saw an execution in any distance of one Muslim man was shot by two soldiers, Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you receive information concerning the general location of where that second execution occurred?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. That was directly east of the bus station area, in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I want to go back a moment to the first report of executions. You referred to an officer who gave the report. Who was that officer, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: First Lieutenant Koster, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: At this time could we have P01516 placed on e-court, please. And if we could zoom in just a touch, please. Perfect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, did Lieutenant Koster describe for you the approximate location where these nine bodies were found?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He described it as a piece of a meadow near the water, brook, like situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And was it close to any particular feature or landmark that you recall?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. Let's say about 100 metres or 80 metres south, south-west of the "White House."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, with Madam Usher's assistance, if I could ask you to just take the stylus and just draw a circle around that general area and if you would write "Nine bodies" and initial and date the document, please?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Okay. As I recollect it, it should have been in this area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge Kwon is suggesting, and I would quite agree, that instead of creating a new document, perhaps he could use the same one he used before on which he put various markings, and that would make things much more practical.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If there's room, absolutely, Your Honour. We can give that a try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm just wondering why my colleague from the Prosecution is getting into hearsay at this time without having established any basis for the need to do so. The person he's referring to is a witness in this case. We will hear first-hand evidence from that witness. What is the need of this point in time to go through a different witness what a real witness is going to come and say? Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Colonel Franken is here. It's relevant evidence. It's corroborative of the testimony that we expect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Objection rejected. This is normal procedure. Mr. Thayer, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to, if I -- with all due respect to the Trial Chamber, ask what is the rationale for the Trial Chamber's decision, because this is hearsay. Hearsay is admissible, but we have to establish some kind of a basis for it and I don't understand why we should hear hearsay evidence when we will here the first-hand evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is not hearsay. This is an internal conversation that took place between this witness and another person and it becomes imperative to have first-hand information or relation from this witness which later on will put us in a position where we can make an assessment when we hear the future -- future evidence of the other officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we are actually, as Judge Kwon rightly points out and we are in agreement here, this is not exactly what one would -- would consider hearsay. This is -- he is repeating the conversation that went on between him and this other person. The other person may or may not confirm it at a later stage, that's true, but this is basically what -- what -- information that he is telling us based on the conversation he had with this other witness. So it's hearsay in -- only in a very limited -- let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could have the document on its head, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if you could draw a circle or -- yes, please draw a circle in the approximate area where Lieutenant Koster reported to you that the bodies had been located.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if you would just write "Nine bodies" and an arrow, please.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we can save the document. Now, sir, again, during this period of time from 12 to 13 July, do you recall receiving any reports from DutchBat soldiers about large numbers of Muslim prisoners being taken outside the enclave?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's as far as I recollect later than the 13th when my -- the crew of OP Alpha was in this period still in position, was brought back over a road north of the enclave, and they reported that they saw a big group of men kneeling on a soccer field or something like that alongside the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall receiving any specific information about how they were around?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. They were in rows and sitting on their knees, hands on their neck.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, again, through the day on the 12th and on the 13th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just for the record, the witness just answered the crew of OP Alpha. Perhaps my colleague from the Prosecution could be more specific on who those members of that crew were that reported this to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, did you understand the question that was posed by my learned colleague?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I'll try to answer it. One of the OPs that was not overtaken or overridden by Serb soldiers in the end phase was the Observation Post A, Alpha. It's on the ultimate west side of the enclave. We were not able to withdraw him with their own means, through -- I mean I remember Jankovic, a Serb officer contacted me, asked for a lorry to bring the -- to pick up the crew of that observation post and bring them back to the location Potocari. Is that an answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. My question would be the specific names of the individuals from DutchBat Jones, Smith, Brown. I want to know if the witness can give us a name or names of the people who gave him this hearsay information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you, Mr. Franken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I cannot, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there a source of information that we could refer to which would have a record of the names of the various officers or members of DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think the NIOD report gives these details. But I don't recollect these names after 11 years, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's quite understandable. All right. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, again during this period of time, the 12th and the 13th, did you observe the living conditions of the refugees changing at all?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. Problem is that we did not have -- it was very hot weather. We were not able to -- to purify water because the lack of fuel. We didn't have any food, and the hygienic situation was, well, disastrous. People didn't have the nerve to go out of their location, as far as I speak now, to the compound itself, out of that factory hall, and -- well, used that hall as a toilet, as a sleeping room, et cetera. Even ladies gave birth in that mess.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: How rapidly, sir, was that humanitarian situation deteriorating?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Very rapidly because we already had death by dehydration, and I coordinated with my doctors, and they said, "Well, two or three days and the problem will solve itself if we can't get -- at least get to water and improve the hygienic situation significantly."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you receive any reports of suicides or suicide attempts, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I recollect two of them. One of them refugees tried to kill themselves by hitting him with a stone on the head. He was stopped by one of my soldiers. One of my officers reported that somebody hanged himself in one of the factory buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I want to it take you from the time period of approximately 14 July through the 16th of July.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You had described previously seeing a pile of personal belongings at a certain distance from the "White House." Did you see what became of those belongings, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. As it was reported to me one of my guards that the pile was on fire. I went down there and looked at it myself, and it was actually burnt, all those possessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'd ask that 65 ter number 1897 be displayed on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you have an image on your screen, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And is it in fact sort of a split -- a split image with two photographs?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I'd ask you when you look at the two photographs whether you recognise what's in one or both of these photographs.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. They were taken from the area of our main gate. Right in the centre of the building that is the so-called "White House" --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And let me just interrupt you for a moment, sir. Which of these images are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: The first one, the upper one.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER FRANKEN
utterances.text: And on the left side is the pile of -- of personal belongings burning we spoke about.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you actually make out the "White House" --
